title: Deliberate Practice
shortDefinition: Deliberate practice means choosing one small cue, measuring results, and increasing resistance step by step.
whyItMatters: Knowing many techniques does not become skill without a feedback loop.
deepExplanation: A good block has static reps, progressive resistance, positional rolling, live testing, and journaling. Each loop asks: which cue worked, which failed, what problem repeated?
beginnerView: Train one small goal across many rounds.
advancedView: Design constraints that force the skill to appear under real pressure.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Deliberate Practice during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Deliberate Practice to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Deliberate Practice is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Deliberate Practice before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
